canonical_facts.publication: Published 1898 (serialised in Pearson's Magazine 1897). Public domain — Project Gutenberg file 36.
canonical_facts.structure: Two books: Book 1 'The Coming of the Martians' (17 chapters), Book 2 'The Earth Under the Martians' (10 chapters).
canonical_facts.setting: Surrey (Woking, Horsell Common, Shepperton, Weybridge, Putney) and London, 1890s.
canonical_facts.narrator: Unnamed, described as a 'professed and recognised writer on philosophical themes' — NOT a scientist. Middle-class, lives in Woking. Married.
canonical_facts.narrators_brother: Unnamed medical student living in London. Describes London evacuation. Rescues Mrs Elphinstone and Miss Elphinstone (sister-in-law of a George Elphinstone) from robbers.
canonical_facts.narrator_wife: Unnamed. Taken to Leatherhead by narrator early in Book 1. Narrator becomes separated from her. They reunite at their home at the end of the novel.
canonical_facts.curate: A Church of England clergyman encountered in Book 1 and trapped with narrator in ruined house in Book 2. His mental state deteriorates over nine days: he hoards food, raves, shouts. On the ninth day the narrator strikes him unconscious with the butt of a meat chopper (turns the blade back). The text is deliberately ambiguous about whether this blow kills him or merely renders him unconscious. A Martian's handling-machine then drags his body away. Chapter title: 'The Death of the Curate' (Book 2, Ch. 4).
canonical_facts.artilleryman: A soldier the narrator meets twice: first in Book 1 (briefly, then travels together towards Weybridge); second in Book 2, Chapter 7 ('The Man on Putney Hill') where he outlines grandiose plans for an underground civilisation, selecting only the 'strong and sane'. His tunnel is barely started — in a week he has done less than a day's work. When the narrator visits, the artilleryman is playing cards and drinking champagne (not wine). Wells's satire of rhetoric without action.
canonical_facts.heat_ray: Described in Book 1, Ch. 5. Exact text: 'An almost noiseless and blinding flash of light'. Effect on people: 'It was as if each man were suddenly and momentarily turned to fire.' It is an invisible beam; only its effects (fire, burning vegetation) are visible.
canonical_facts.thunder_child: HMS Thunder Child — a torpedo ram (ironclad warship). Appears in Book 1, Ch. 17. Charges three Martian tripods to protect refugee ships heading to France. Destroys TWO tripods (first with guns, second by ramming) before being sunk by the Heat-Ray. The brother witnesses this from a refugee boat.
canonical_facts.black_smoke: A chemical weapon — poisonous gas that settles on the ground. Kills all life it contacts. Not simply 'gas' — it is a specific cloud that settles as a black deposit.
canonical_facts.red_weed: Alien plant brought by Martians. Spreads over rivers and landscape, turning them crimson. Eventually dies (killed by bacteria just as the Martians are).
canonical_facts.martian_appearance: Exact text: 'huge round bodies—or, rather, heads—about four feet in diameter, each body having in front of it a face.' Two large dark eyes, a V-shaped beak-like mouth, two groups of eight tentacles. No digestive system — they feed by injecting blood directly into their own veins using a pipette-like mechanism.
canonical_facts.martian_feeding: Martians have no digestive organs. They feed by mechanically injecting the blood of living creatures (including humans) directly into their veins. This is how Earth's bacteria enter their systems and kill them.
canonical_facts.martians_death: Killed by Earth's bacteria (putrefactive and disease bacteria) against which they have no immunity, having eliminated disease on Mars. The exact quote is: 'slain by the putrefactive and disease bacteria against which their systems were unprepared; slain as the red weed was being slain; slain, after all man's devices had failed, by the humblest things that God, in his wisdom, has put upon this earth.' Note the important first clause 'after all man's devices had failed' is commonly omitted in GCSE resources.
canonical_facts.tasmanian_quote: Exact text from Book 1, Ch. 1: 'And before we judge of them too harshly we must remember what ruthless and utter destruction our own species has wrought, not only upon animals, such as the vanished bison and the dodo, but upon its inferior races.' GCSE lessons commonly shorten to 'Before we judge them too harshly...' — omits 'of' and 'And', acceptable as paraphrase.
canonical_facts.london_exodus_quote: 'Never before in the history of the world had such a mass of human beings moved and suffered together.' — confirmed in text. Also: 'the roaring wave of fear that swept through the greatest city in the world' (Book 1, Ch. 16).
canonical_facts.wells_beliefs: Wells's religious position was complex and evolving. In 1898 he was broadly anti-clerical and a freethinker, moving towards atheism but not straightforwardly described as 'an atheist' — he later published a religious tract ('God the Invisible King', 1917) before repudiating it. Calling him simply 'an atheist' is a simplification; 'agnostic' or 'freethinker' is more accurate for 1898.
canonical_facts.artilleryman_drinks: The artilleryman drinks champagne (not wine). Text confirms: 'the artilleryman finished the champagne' in Book 2, Ch. 7.
canonical_facts.brother_occupation: The narrator's brother is a medical student — confirmed correct.
canonical_facts.narrator_occupation: A writer of philosophical papers — not a scientist. His scientific literacy comes from general education, not a scientific career.
canonical_facts.narration_retrospective: The narrator writes retrospectively — he is looking back on events that have already happened. Wells uses this to combine immediacy of experience with analytical hindsight.

issues.claim: 'huge round bodies—or rather heads—about four feet in diameter, each body having in front of it a face.'
issues.correct: The exact text is 'huge round bodies—or, rather, heads—about four feet in diameter, each body having in front of it a face.' The lesson's version omits the comma after 'or' but is otherwise correct and acceptable as a GCSE quotation.

issues.claim: A deputation approaches the cylinder waving a white flag. The Martians respond with the Heat-Ray, killing them instantly.
issues.correct: Accurate in substance. The deputation included Ogilvy (astronomer), Henderson (journalist) and Stent (Astronomer Royal). Saying 'a deputation' without naming them is acceptable for GCSE scope.

issues.claim: The Martian Heat-Ray is described as an invisible beam that sets everything it touches on fire. Wells never explains the science.
issues.correct: Accurate. The original text describes 'An almost noiseless and blinding flash of light' — the lesson does not misquote, merely paraphrases accurately.

issues.claim: It destroys two tripods before being overwhelmed.
issues.correct: Confirmed correct — the Thunder Child destroys two Martian tripods (one with guns, one by ramming) before being sunk. No error.

issues.claim: the Hague Convention of 1899 attempted to ban poison gas
issues.correct: The Hague Convention of 1899 did not specifically ban poison gas — that was the 1925 Geneva Protocol. The 1899 Hague Declaration (IV, 2) banned the use of projectiles 'the sole object of which is the diffusion of asphyxiating or deleterious gases.' This is a minor contextual imprecision. The novel was published in 1898, so the convention was still in the future — the lesson's framing implies Wells was drawing on an existing convention, when he was anticipating one.

issues.claim: he spends his time drinking champagne and playing cards
issues.correct: Confirmed correct — the text says 'the artilleryman finished the champagne.' No error here. However, the lesson places the artilleryman encounter as happening 'after escaping' the ruined house, which is correct chronologically (Book 2, Ch. 7 follows the curate episode in Book 2, Ch. 4). Accurate.

issues.claim: The narrator is forced to knock him unconscious.
issues.correct: This is accurate but simplifies the novel's deliberate ambiguity. The chapter is titled 'The Death of the Curate' and it is unclear whether the blow kills him or merely renders him unconscious before the Martians take his body. The lesson might benefit from acknowledging this ambiguity as it is analytically important for AO2.

issues.claim: Wells, an atheist, uses the curate to argue that religion is inadequate in the face of genuine existential threat.
issues.correct: Wells's religious position was evolving and complex. At the time of the novel (1898) he was broadly anti-clerical and a freethinker. Calling him definitively 'an atheist' is a simplification — he published a religious tract ('God the Invisible King') in 1917 before repudiating it, and was more accurately described as agnostic or freethinker. This label also recurs in OCR L7. At GCSE level it is commonly used as shorthand, but 'agnostic' or 'freethinker' is more precise.

issues.claim: The narrator's brother provides an alternative viewpoint of the London evacuation (Book 1, Chapters 14–17).
issues.correct: Confirmed accurate. The brother's narrative spans Book 1, Chapters 14–17. No error.

issues.claim: The shift from the narrator to his brother in Book 1 Chapters 14–17 is a structural innovation.
issues.correct: Confirmed accurate — the brother's narrative runs through Book 1, Chapters 14–17. No error.

issues.location: Religion under pressure collapsible, n8 — Wells described as 'an atheist'
issues.claim: Wells, an atheist, suggests that religious frameworks are inadequate when confronted with a universe that is indifferent to human suffering.
issues.correct: Same issue as OCR L5: calling Wells simply 'an atheist' is a simplification. See L5 note. At GCSE this is common shorthand but 'freethinker' or 'agnostic' is more accurate for 1898.

issues.claim: This is typically a closed-text exam.
issues.correct: For OCR J352, the exam is closed-book (no text in the hall) but an extract from the set text IS printed on the exam question paper. Saying 'closed-text' could mislead students into thinking they must work entirely from memory with no passage provided. The OCR format is extract-based: students analyse a printed extract AND make wider reference. The lesson does add 'Check your exam board's specimen paper' as a caveat, which partially mitigates this.

issues.claim: 'slain by the humblest things that God, in his wisdom, has put upon this earth' (bacteria)
issues.correct: This is a partial quotation. The full sentence begins: 'slain, after all man's devices had failed, by the humblest things that God, in his wisdom, has put upon this earth.' The first clause 'after all man's devices had failed' is analytically crucial — it establishes that the bacteria ending undercuts human agency, not just celebrates bacterial life. Students quoting only the truncated version miss a key AO2 point.

issues.claim: 'By ten o'clock the police organisation was lost in the growing pressure of the flight' — civilisation's collapse.
issues.correct: This quote cannot be verified precisely against the text but is plausible. The wording is consistent with the novel's documentary style and the Book 1 exodus chapters. No confirmed error, flagged as unverified.

issues.claim: 'Before we judge [the Martians] too harshly, we must remember what ruthless and utter destruction our own species has wrought, not only upon animals — but upon its inferior races.'
issues.correct: The exact text reads: 'And before we judge of them too harshly we must remember what ruthless and utter destruction our own species has wrought, not only upon animals, such as the vanished bison and the dodo, but upon its inferior races.' The lesson's version inserts '[the Martians]', omits 'of' after 'judge', and abbreviates the middle clause with an em dash. The substituted '[the Martians]' for 'them' is a clarification not an error. The abbreviation of the animals clause ('not only upon animals — but') loses the specific examples of bison and dodo that Wells includes, which are analytically significant. Low severity at GCSE but students should know the fuller quote.

issues.claim: 'It was as if each man were suddenly and momentarily turned to fire.'
issues.correct: Confirmed correct against the original text (Book 1, Ch. 5). No error.

issues.claim: The narrator's psychological realism section (n12) and a separate paragraph (n16) describe the same idea with near-identical language: 'He admits that his mind kept returning to "the normal"...' and 'He admits that his mind kept returning to "the normal"...'
issues.correct: The paragraph beginning 'The narrator himself struggles to comprehend what is happening...' (n16) repeats the content of n12 almost verbatim. This is a copy-paste duplication rather than a factual error, but it weakens the lesson's quality and could confuse students studying the content carefully.
issues.source: Internal — content duplication between n12 and n16 in this lesson's HTML

lessons.title: Book 1 Continued: The Fall of Civilisation

issues.claim: It manages to destroy one tripod before being sunk.
issues.correct: The Thunder Child destroys TWO Martian tripods — first with its guns, then by ramming the second with its flaming wreckage. Multiple sources confirm this. The lesson says 'one tripod', which is incorrect. This directly contradicts the correct account in OCR L3 (which says two), so one of the two boards has an error. The Eduqas version is wrong.

issues.claim: the brother describes 'the roaring wave of fear that swept through the greatest city in the world'
issues.correct: Confirmed correct against the original text (Book 1, Ch. 16). No error.

issues.claim: The destruction of HMS Thunder Child is the most dramatic military engagement in the novel.
issues.correct: Accurate description but the lesson says it 'manages to destroy one tripod' — see error note above.

issues.claim: The narrator is forced to knock him unconscious.
issues.correct: Accurate but the lesson goes on in n3 to say 'When the narrator finally strikes him, it is an act of pragmatic necessity' — this is analytically sound. The lesson does not claim the narrator kills the curate outright; the phrasing 'knock him unconscious' is appropriate. However, the chapter is titled 'The Death of the Curate', and the text's ambiguity about whether the blow kills him or the Martians take him alive is an important analytical point that could be developed for AO2.

issues.claim: 'slain by the humblest things that God, in his wisdom, has put upon this earth'
issues.correct: Truncated. The full sentence begins: 'slain, after all man's devices had failed, by the humblest things that God, in his wisdom, has put upon this earth.' The omitted clause is analytically significant. Same issue as OCR L8.

issues.claim: But his tunnel is barely started. Wells uses him as a satire of people who respond to crisis with big talk and no action.
issues.correct: The content is accurate in calling the tunnel barely started. However, earlier in the same lesson (n9) it states he 'plays cards and drinks wine'. The artilleryman drinks champagne — the text explicitly says 'the artilleryman finished the champagne' (Book 2, Ch. 7). 'Wine' is incorrect.

issues.claim: He kills the curate (or at least strikes him unconscious, leading to his death).
issues.correct: This is the most accurate account of the curate episode in any of the 16 lessons — the parenthetical '(or at least strikes him unconscious, leading to his death)' correctly represents the textual ambiguity. No error; note this as the model phrasing for other lessons.

issues.claim: Book 1: The Coming of the Martians (large-scale invasion, military response, societal collapse) and Book 2: The Earth Under the Martians (personal survival, underground hiding, encounters with curate and artilleryman, resolution).
issues.correct: Confirmed accurate — correct titles, correct structural description. No error.

issues.claim: The Martians, despite their intelligence, lack one crucial adaptation — immunity to Earth's microbes — and this kills them.
issues.correct: Accurate. No error.

issues.claim: The richest passages for analysis: (1) The opening chapter with Tasmanian reference. (2) The Heat-Ray scene on Horsell Common. (3) The London exodus. (4) HMS Thunder Child's destruction. (5) The narrator trapped with the curate. (6) The bacteria ending.
issues.correct: All six passage descriptions are accurate. No factual errors.

issues.claim: 'the humblest things' as an ironic commentary on human pride
issues.correct: Analytically sound. No factual error. This lesson does not quote the truncated version — it analyses the phrase conceptually rather than quoting it, so the truncation issue from other lessons does not apply here.
